headline: UK Net Migration Falls to 77,000, Its Lowest Level Since 1997
subheadline: Provisional ONS figures for the year to June 2026 show net migration more than halved in a year, driven by fewer non-EU arrivals for work and study — with Indians still the largest non-EU nationality coming to Britain.
body:
• Net migration to the UK fell to a provisional 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, down from 204,000 a year earlier — the lowest figure since 1997, excluding the pandemic years.
  • The fall was driven by non-EU nationals, whose net migration dropped to 258,000 from 379,000 as arrivals for work and study declined.
  • Indian nationals remained the most common non-EU nationality both arriving in and leaving the UK, with study the most common reason for coming.
  • For readers weighing a UK move: study routes still account for 47% of non-EU arrivals, but work-related arrivals fell 25% in a year — the door is narrower, not closed.

Net migration to the United Kingdom fell to 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, the lowest level recorded since 1997 outside the coronavirus pandemic, according to provisional figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) on Thursday. The figure is down from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 and continues a steep decline from the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.

An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK long term in the year to June 2026, a fall of 17% from 893,000 a year earlier, while emigration was broadly stable at 661,000, the ONS said. Net migration counts people moving for 12 months or more.

What drove the fall

The decrease was driven almost entirely by nationals from outside the EU. Non-EU net migration fell to 258,000 from 379,000, because arrivals dropped by more than 100,000 while departures held steady. Compared with a year earlier, non-EU arrivals for work-related reasons fell by 45,000, study-related arrivals fell by 33,000 and asylum-related arrivals fell by 19,000.

Study remained the largest single route. Of the 550,000 non-EU nationals who arrived in the year to June 2026, 47% came for study-related reasons, 25% for work and 13% for asylum-related reasons. Study arrivals totalled 257,000, down 11% on the year, with main applicants down 12% to 242,000 and dependants stable at 15,000. Work arrivals fell 25% to 135,000; main applicants dropped 30% to 60,000 and work dependants fell 21% to 75,000.

Net migration for British nationals was negative 137,000 and for EU nationals negative 45,000, meaning more people in both groups left the UK long term than arrived.

"In 2026, non-EU citizens are the only group driving positive net migration."

— Sarah Crofts, ONS deputy director of migration statistics

The Indian picture

Indian was the most common non-EU nationality among people immigrating long term to the UK in the year ending June 2026, according to the ONS, continuing a pattern in which Indian, Pakistani, Chinese and Nigerian nationals are regularly among the top five. Study was the most common reason for arrival among the leading nationalities.

Indians also topped the list of non-EU nationals leaving. Of the 292,000 non-EU nationals who emigrated, around 53% had originally arrived on study-related visas, and the ONS said the 155,000 departures of people who first came to study likely reflect the large student cohorts of 2022 and 2023 completing their studies and post-study work periods.

Reaction and what happens next

The government said it had brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives. Reuters reported that the figures ease political pressure on the government, though the sharp fall in arrivals could hinder parts of the economy that rely on overseas workers.

The estimates are provisional and typically remain so for about a year. The ONS cautioned that its British-national figures for this release rest on an extended 15-month projection because updated data were unavailable, so they carry greater uncertainty than usual and may be revised in the next release.
